newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lower, corporate supply a drag.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lower, corporate supply a drag.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower on Thursday in a technically-driven session, dragged down by some post-auction selling and a large amount of fresh corporate supply, analysts said.
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 4/32 at 101-2/32. Its yield rose slightly to 6.42 percent.

"Generally people wanted to buy the market on dips. We tried to go to the highs twice but there wasn't a lot of follow through," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist of fixed-income at C.S. First Boston.
"There was also a lot of corporate paper coming to market and that's in fact what brought the market down at the end of the day," Alexy added.
Bond traders said some $2.1 billion in new corporate debt issuance hit the market on Thursday. That number adds to roughly $2.7 billion in corporate debt issued the day before.
Prices see-sawed within narrow ranges throughout the session as technicals outweighed fundamentals after investors shrugged off most of the freshly-released economic data.
The economic indicator log for Thursday included a 344,000 rise in jobless claims in the week ended November 16 against a revised 327,000 number in the previous period.
Although a rise in claims is usually seen as a positive for the market, players paid little attention to it.

By mid-morning, the market took in a rise in the Philadelphia Federal Reserve index to 6.4 in November against 5.3 in October. The report's prices paid component, however, fell to 14.6 in November against 21.9 earlier.

"The indicators didn't aid a whole lot today. The most interesting thing was in the Philly Fed report. We did have the weakness in prices, which was encouraging," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
Analysts said they noticed some resistance forming in the area around 6.40 percent in the long-end of the yield curve.
Bonds tested that level early in the session when the benchmark yielded 6.39 percent for a brief period just to climb back up moments later.
"It seems the market got a bit stalled at these levels ... And I guess we're likely to see more consolidation over the next few days," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Dealers were also seen distributing securities after the auctions of two- and five-year Treasury notes earlier in the week, when the Treasury sold some $30 billion in supply.
"Dealers were trying to unload some of the paper they took in," said another trader at a U.S. bank.
The fact that Treasuries remained relatively stable amid the recent flood of supply was a sign that the market continues to be bullish going forward.
"I don't think the market is going to go much further between now and year-end. But we're still looking for a 5-1/2 30-year Treasury (yield) in the middle of next year," DLJ's Platt said.
Trading was said to be dominated by professionals on Thursday. Neither retailers nor hedge and mutual funds were seen active on the market.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up one basis point at 5.03 percent. The six-month bill rate rose one point to 5.06 percent. The year bill rate was up two points at 5.14 percent.

The two-year note closed down 1/32 at 99-29/32, yielding 5.67 percent. The five-year note traded off 2/32 at 99-24/32 to yield 5.93 percent. The ten-year note closed down 1/32 at 102-21/32, yielding 6.14 percent.
